| [NOTE-649](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-649.md) | Large AI models are cultural and social technologies | Argues that large models are a cultural and social technology, not intelligent agents: lossy, uninvertible summaries of human-produced corpora that, like prices and bureaucratic categories, allow the information to be reorganized at scale. | [NOTE-697](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-697.md) | Floridi — AI as agency without intelligence | An editorial, not an argument. LLMs work statistically on the form of texts and understand nothing, yet they act successfully and, through RL fine-tuning, "learn" to act better. Floridi concludes that they are "a new form of agency" that has been "liberated … from intelligence" (pp. 5–6). Learning to make "a different or better difference" is the only mark given that separates it from a sea wave. The no-understanding premise rests on anecdote, and no criteria for agency are stated. | Read |
| [NOTE-702](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-702.md) | Floridi — AI as agency without intelligence and the MRA thesis | A taxonomy, not an argument for its thesis. The case for the Multiple Realisability of Agency over the Artificial Realisability of Intelligence is announced (evidence, common sense, Ockham, literature) and then set aside: the paper assumes AI is an agent and asks what kind (p. 2). Floridi & Sanders' three criteria come back, loosened, so that interactivity alone makes a river a "natural agent" (p. 9). The criteria do not separate AI from other artefacts. Origin, mechanism, where the goals come from, and asserted absences (no intelligence, no mental states) do that. No level of abstraction is ever specified. | Read |
| [NOTE-745](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-745.md) | Susser, Roessler and Nissenbaum — Technology, autonomy, and manipulation | Defines manipulation as intentionally and covertly influencing a person's decision-making by targeting and exploiting their decision-making vulnerabilities, with attempted covertness as the essential feature. | [NOTE-1026](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1026.md) | Perzanowski and Schultz — The End of Ownership | Ownership of what we buy is being replaced by licences, DRM and services. | [NOTE-1052](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1052.md) | Arthur — Competing technologies and historical small events (working paper) | In a model where two types of agent arrive in random order and each adopts whichever of two technologies pays it more, with returns linear in the number of previous adopters, increasing returns make the difference in adoptions a random walk with absorbing barriers: one technology takes the market with probability one, which one is decided by the order of arrivals, it need not be the better one, and marginal subsidies cannot move it once it has locked in. | [NOTE-1096](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1096.md) | Flayelle et al. — A taxonomy of technology design features that promote potentially addictive online behaviours | A narrative review and a taxonomy. Design features of six kinds of online service are linked, mostly by cross-sectional, qualitative or indirect evidence, to loss of control. They are sorted by the learning and control process each exploits. Model-free: reinforcement schedules and personalized triggers. Model-based: overvaluation, interference with deliberation, partial goal fulfilment, cognitive biases. Providers select features by their effect on use and revenue, and personalize them under informational asymmetry. For the record it maps closely onto the parts of the potential account: features that strengthen a cue-keyed ranking, move its reference course, falsify the user's reading of progress, or pre-empt the other perspectives. | Read |
| [NOTE-1710](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1710.md) | Macnamara et al. — AI assistance, skill decay and awareness | A theoretical perspective with no data. Skill decays with disuse, more for cognitive than physical tasks; disuse can be partial, a subtask ceased while automation does it and the task goes on; in Casner et al.'s pilots, reported second-hand, procedural flying skills held while cognitive skills declined; and such decay is concealed because the task is still done and still succeeds with the support. AI assistants, which take over more cognitive work, are predicted to do this more; the authors say no research has tested it. | Read |

| [NOTE-1792](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1792.md) | Étienne Brown — Recommended Selves: Authenticity and Algorithmic Filtering | Brown argues that recommender systems affect users' capacity to be their authentic selves, both negatively and positively. He offers a "minimal", multi-dimensional account of authenticity with two dimensions: volitional alignment (Frankfurt, via Rings: acting on first-order desires one reflectively endorses at second order) and self-understanding (an epistemic dimension, relational rather than purely introspective: others' testimony and recommendations are a source of self-knowledge). Recommenders frustrate volitional alignment "by design", because they rank on behavioural signals (clicks, dwell time) that, following Sen, cannot reveal second-order desires; the manipulation and digital-addiction literatures (Susser, Roessler and Nissenbaum; Allcott, Gentzkow and Song) are cited as two forms of this. But recommenders can foster self-understanding by showing users whom they behave like (the Hao and Ellie House cases, users realizing their bisexuality), against Doyle's objection to "listening to algorithms", which Brown limits to pure deference. Opacity is the danger: the Farah case, where content is recommended for location not behaviour and she draws a false conclusion about herself. Remedies: user control (surveys, middleware, conversational recommenders, LLM "attention guardians") for volitional alignment, and explainable recommenders that say which similarity relation drove a recommendation, for self-understanding; with a tension: too much control may remove the encounters that prompt self-discovery. | Read |
